t.5.7.1: In the midst of that most excellent of dwellings, Hanūmān, the son of the Wind-god, beheld the finest of mansions, vast and far-extending.
t.5.7.2: That palace of the lord of the rākṣasas, crowded with many mansions, was indeed half a yojana in breadth and a yojana in length.
t.5.7.3: But Hanūmān, the destroyer of foes, searching for Sītā, the princess of Videha with large, long eyes, roamed about everywhere.
t.5.7.4: It was surrounded by elephants with four tusks and likewise with three tusks; spacious and uncrowded, it was guarded by warriors with upraised weapons.
t.5.7.5: The dwelling of Rāvaṇa was thronged with his rākṣasī wives and with the daughters of kings whom he had carried off by force.
t.5.7.7: Whatever splendor dwells in Vaiśravaṇa, and whatever in Indra, whose steeds are bay horses, all of it abides in Rāvaṇa's house, constant and never departing.
t.5.7.6: He beheld that palace as if it were the ocean, strewn with crocodiles and makaras, teeming with timiṅgilas and fish, tossed by the force of the wind, and filled, as it were, with serpents.
t.5.7.8: Whatever prosperity belongs to King Kubera, to Yama and to Varuṇa, such prosperity, or even greater than that, is here in the houses of the Rākṣasas.
t.5.7.9: And in the midst of that palace the son of the Wind beheld another dwelling, finely built and crowded with many turrets.
t.5.7.10: The divine aerial chariot named Puṣpaka, adorned with every kind of jewel, which Viśvakarman had fashioned in heaven for the sake of Brahmā.
t.5.7.11: That which Kubera had obtained from the Grandsire through supreme austerity, the lord of the Rākṣasas obtained by conquering Kubera with his might.
t.5.7.13: It was adorned on every side with upper chambers of beautiful form, resembling Meru and Mandara, which seemed to scrape the sky.
t.5.7.12: It was set with well-wrought pillars of pure gold adorned with figures of wolves, and it seemed to blaze with splendor.
t.5.7.14: It shone like fire and the sun, was skilfully fashioned by Viśvakarman, was furnished with golden stairways, and had lovely, excellent terraces.
t.5.7.15: The great monkey climbed onto the divine aerial chariot Puṣpaka, fitted with latticed windows of gold and of crystal, and adorned with platforms of the finest gems, sapphires and great sapphires.
t.5.7.16: Standing there, he then smelled the divine fragrance, arising from drinks, delicacies and food, spread all around, like the wind itself having taken on bodily form.
t.5.7.17: That fragrance, like a kinsman to an excellent kinsman, seemed to say to that being of great strength, "Come here, this way," toward the place where Rāvaṇa was.
t.5.7.18: Then, having set out, he beheld that great and splendid hall, dear to the heart of Rāvaṇa, like a beloved and most excellent woman.
t.5.7.19: It was fashioned with jewelled stairways and resplendent with golden latticework; its floors were overlaid with crystal, and figures were set amid inlays of ivory.
t.5.7.20: He saw it adorned with pearls and coral, with silver and gold as well, decorated with jewelled pillars and embellished with a great many columns.
t.5.7.21: With its even, straight and very lofty pillars, richly adorned on every side, it seemed, as if borne on towering wings, to be setting out for heaven.
t.5.7.22: He beheld the floor, spread with a great carpet emblazoned with the features of the earth, vast as the earth itself and garlanded with kingdoms and houses.
t.5.7.23: He saw it resounding with the cries of intoxicated birds, perfumed with heavenly fragrances, furnished with the costliest coverings, and frequented by the lord of the Rākṣasas.
t.5.7.24: It was smoky grey with the fumes of agaru incense, yet spotless and white as a swan; variegated with offerings of flowers, it shone brilliantly, as though dappled.
t.5.7.25: He beheld that divine one, which brought delight to the mind and brightened even the complexion, which destroyed sorrow and was like the very source of splendour.
t.5.7.27: "This is heaven, this is the world of the gods, this must be the city of Indra, or else this must be the supreme perfection," so thought Māruti.
t.5.7.26: Then, guarded by Rāvaṇa, she gratified the five senses with the five finest objects of the senses, like a mother.
t.5.7.28: There he saw golden lamps, still as though belonging to one lost in brooding thought, like gamblers beaten at dice by master cheats.
t.5.7.29: By the light of the lamps, by the splendour of Rāvaṇa, and by the radiance of the ornaments, he thought it to be ablaze.
t.5.7.30: Then he saw a thousand excellent women seated upon carpets, wearing garments and garlands of many colours and adorned with many kinds of attire.
t.5.7.31: When midnight had passed, the throng of women, having fallen under the sway of drink and sleep, and having ceased after sporting through the night, then slept soundly.
t.5.7.32: That sleeping throng, its ornaments now silent, shone like a great forest of lotuses in which the swans and bees have fallen silent.
t.5.7.33: Māruti saw the faces of those lovely women, their teeth concealed behind closed lips and their eyes shut, faces fragrant as the lotus.
t.5.7.34: Their lotuses, which at the end of night had been as if fully blossomed, then shone like lotuses whose petals had closed again, as at night.
t.5.7.35: Surely the intoxicated bees seek these lotus-faces again and again, as if they were full-blown lotuses.
t.5.7.37: That hall of his, made resplendent by those women, shone like the clear autumn sky adorned with stars.
t.5.7.36: So, or so it seemed, the glorious great monkey reasoned it out; for by their qualities he deemed them equal to the water-born lotuses.
t.5.7.38: And that lord of the Rākṣasas, surrounded by those women, shone forth just as the glorious lord of the stars, the moon, shines when encircled by the stars.
t.5.7.39: "The stars that fall from the sky, still enveloped by what remains of their merit, these are they, all gathered here together," so the monkey thought then.
t.5.7.40: There the radiance, complexion and clear beauty of the women shone forth distinctly, like those of great stars of auspicious brilliance.
t.5.7.41: Their heavy, full garlands twisted aside and their fine ornaments scattered, the women lay with their minds stolen away by sleep, overcome in the hours of drinking and amorous exertion.
t.5.7.42: Some of those most excellent women had their tilaka marks smudged, some had their anklets slipped out of place, and some had their necklaces fallen to one side.
t.5.7.43: Others were adorned with strings of pearls, and some had their garments slipped loose, their girdle-strings flung awry, like young mares that have been ridden hard and unharnessed.
t.5.7.44: And other women, wearing beautiful earrings, their garlands torn and crushed, lay like blossoming creepers trampled by a lordly elephant in a great forest.
t.5.7.45: And the splendid necklaces of some of the women, gleaming like the rays of the moon, shone between their breasts like sleeping swans.
t.5.7.46: The beryl ornaments of some were like kādamba birds, and the golden chains of others became like cakravāka birds.
t.5.7.47: Strewn as if with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks and adorned as if with cakravāka birds, those women shone like rivers, their hips like sandbanks.
t.5.7.48: Those women, glittering with networks of tiny bells, with their gold ornaments as broad lotuses, their passions as crocodiles and their fame as banks, shone like sleeping rivers.
t.5.7.49: On the soft limbs and on the tips of the breasts of some of the women, the lovely lines left by their ornaments lay imprinted and seemed like ornaments themselves.
t.5.7.50: And the lovely silken threads of some of the women, stirred by the breath of their mouths, are tossed up again and again just above their faces.
t.5.7.51: Like banners tossed aloft, those things of lovely radiance shone at the base of the wives' faces, amid their golden ornaments of many hues.
t.5.7.53: The breath from the mouths of those women, fragrant by nature and pleasant, carrying the scent of sugar-cane liquor, then wafted over Rāvaṇa.
t.5.7.52: And here the earrings of some of those lovely women, bright with radiant splendour, stirred gently, ever so gently, at the touch of the breath from their mouths.
t.5.7.55: Those noble women, their hearts excessively attached to Rāvaṇa, being not their own mistresses, then did only what was pleasing to their co-wives.
t.5.7.54: And some of Rāvaṇa's women, taking them for Rāvaṇa's face, kissed the faces of their co-wives again and again.
t.5.7.56: Other young women there, adorned with bracelets, lay sleeping, having placed their arms and their lovely garments beneath them as pillows.
t.5.7.57: One woman lay upon the breast of another, and some other, in turn, upon that one's arm; another rested on the lap of yet another, and still another upon her two arms.
t.5.7.58: Resting on one another's thighs, sides, hips and backs, their limbs intertwined with each other, they lay overcome by intoxication and affection.
t.5.7.59: Delighted by the touch of one another's bodies, all those slender-waisted women slept there with their arms intertwined.
t.5.7.60: That garland of women, strung together by the thread of one another's arms, shone like a garland strung on a thread and swarming with intoxicated bees.
t.5.7.61: It was interwoven, garland with garland, a mass of clinging blossoms, like the creepers that flower in the month of Mādhava when they are stirred by the wind.
t.5.7.62: That grove of Rāvaṇa's women, their fine shoulders closely intertwined and thronged with bees moving from one to another, was like a forest tossed by the wind, its sturdy trunks entwined together.
t.5.7.63: Even where they lay in their proper places, it was then impossible to clearly tell apart the ornaments, limbs, garments and garlands of those women.
t.5.7.64: While Rāvaṇa lay comfortably asleep, there lay those women of varied radiance, and the blazing golden lamps seemed to gaze upon them without blinking.
t.5.7.65: The women of royal sages, Pitṛs, Daityas and Gandharvas, and the maidens of the Rākṣasas, had come under the sway of his desire.
t.5.7.66: No woman there had been seized by force; each had been won by his merit joined with valor. None of them longed for another, nor had any belonged to another before, except the daughter of Janaka, who was worthy of the noblest.
t.5.7.67: No wife of his was of low birth or lacking in beauty, none was unskilled or wanting in gracious conduct, none was feeble in spirit, and none was undesirable to her beloved lord.
t.5.7.68: Then this thought arose in the lord of the monkeys, whose mind was virtuous: “If the lawful wife of Rāghava is such as these wives of the king of the Rākṣasas are, then it is truly well for him.”
t.5.7.69: And again he, distressed in appearance, reflected: "Surely Sītā is superior by virtue of her qualities; and yet this great-souled lord of Laṅkā has done to her a grievous, ignoble deed."
